prize_parts.citation: for incorporating firm heterogeneity into trade theory, showing how selection into exporting and reallocation across firms generate gains from trade

statement.case_for: The heterogeneous-firm framework changed the unit of analysis in international economics from the industry to the firm. It gives a single mechanism, selection and reallocation across firms of different productivity, that explains exporter premia, who exports versus who serves markets through FDI, and a channel for gains from trade that comparative advantage and representative-firm models miss. Melitz (2003) is the clear origin. Helpman's contributions, notably Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple on exporting versus FDI, turned the idea into a broader research programme. More than twenty years of theory, structural quantification and firm-level microdata support it. It also spread to other fields: the reallocation logic now informs work on productivity, growth and the effects of policy on aggregate outcomes. Attribution to two named people is comparatively tight, and the area has not been recognised since Krugman's 2008 prize, which covered earlier trade theory built on increasing returns and location.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is attribution. Bernard, Eaton, Jensen and Kortum produced parallel and empirical antecedents that are not on this ballot entry, and Redding is a significant later contributor who would be omitted under a two-name credit. Some of the welfare results depend on functional-form assumptions, and in the quantitative trade tradition (see B031) simpler gravity and Ricardian models give similar aggregate gains. A committee could read the contribution as overlapping with the 2008 prize on trade. Compared with B001, the case also rests more on a conceptual framework and less on a toolkit that is routinely used in regulatory practice.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B050 third and asks whether Melitz alone or Melitz with Helpman is the stronger framing, noting that Helpman's record spans several candidacies (B021 and B050), that Redding is more recent, and that the 2008 prize covered earlier trade theory. He also proposes limiting B002 to Kiyotaki and Moore because of the Bernanke-Gertler-Gilchrist overlap with the 2022 prize.
responses.response: I would keep Helpman in the credit. The Helpman-Melitz-Yeaple work on exporting versus FDI is a constitutive part of the firm-heterogeneity achievement, not a side strand. I would not let the protection-for-sale work in B021 enter the credit for this prize, since it is a separate achievement. On B002, I find his two-name proposal persuasive. Kiyotaki-Moore is the clean originating contribution, and adding Gertler imports the Bernanke overlap. I would qualify my opening three-name proposal accordingly if B002 is taken up. I disclose below that Krusell is a frequent co-author.

responses.point: Dreber ranks B001 first. She argues that BLP demand estimation and dynamic-oligopoly methods are the standard toolkit for merger review, antitrust and empirical IO, with three decades of stress-testing, and that numerical sensitivity and weak identification are well documented and largely addressed.
responses.response: I did not rank B001 in my opening, and that reflects my distance from the field more than a judgment on merit. I find the maturity and adoption arguments persuasive, and the spread of the methods into trade, production-function estimation and markup measurement is real. I now treat B001 as a close alternative. My remaining reservations are about the unit of the prize, since demand estimation, production-function methods and dynamic games are distinct strands, and about the attribution cut among seven credited names, where the Bresnahan versus Levinsohn choice is not settled. B050 has its own omissions, but it is a single idea with a clearer founder. I would not move B001 ahead of it on the basis of support counts alone.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B050 second and credits Melitz (2003) as the pivotal contribution, with Helpman's heterogeneous-firm, FDI and trade-and-politics work fitting the same theme. He notes that Redding is more recent and that Helpman's other candidacy (B021) could complicate the allocation of credit.
responses.response: I agree on Melitz as the pivot and on a two-person split with Helpman. I would add that the allocation concern is manageable if the citation is tied tightly to firm heterogeneity and selection. That keeps Helpman's political-economy work out of scope and leaves B021 as a separate matter. His point about Bernard, Eaton and Kortum is the real attribution risk. It is a genuine cost of the two-name design, and I would not claim the ballot entry resolves it.

responses.point: Fredriksson ranks B002 first and B050 seventh. On B050 he stresses that Krugman's earlier prize covered an earlier generation of trade theory, so the incremental contribution must be argued, and that gains-from-trade quantification depends on model specification.
responses.response: I accept that the incremental argument has to be made. My answer is that Krugman's prize covered increasing returns, monopolistic competition and location, while firm heterogeneity added selection, reallocation and a firm-level empirical agenda. The overlap is thematic, not in the substance of the discovery. I also accept that quantitative gains depend on model specification, though the qualitative selection and reallocation margins have held up in microdata. On B002, I share his view that the collateral-amplification mechanism is deep and mature. I rank it second behind B050 because of the 2022 overlap and the awkward credit among Gertler, Gilchrist and Bernanke.

uncertainties: Whether the committee should name Redding or the Bernard-Eaton-Jensen-Kortum group, which are outside this ballot entry, in the heterogeneous-firm credit.
How far the 2008 trade prize reduces appetite for another trade award.
Whether the many ballot-level first-place rankings for B001 reflect an attribution and maturity case that I have underweighted, given that I did not rank it in my opening.
For B002, whether Gertler belongs in the credit given the Bernanke prize in 2022.
I rely on background knowledge for citation and adoption evidence and have not independently verified any of it.
statement.conflict_note: From the supplied profile: I am a long-time co-author of Peter Klenow, who is credited on B039, which is not in my preferred configuration. I also have a long-running collaboration with Aghion, Bergeaud and Li, who do not appear on this shortlist. Per Krusell (secretary) is a frequent co-author and John Hassler (chair) a co-author, and I am an IIES colleague of both. They are committee colleagues, not candidates. No tie to Melitz, Helpman or Redding is apparent from the supplied profile. These connections are disclosed, not adjudicated.
